Areas In Reg Poly

AreaGeometryTriangles
Game: Drag the dot inside the polygon and watch the two colours of triangles: their areas always add up to the same total. There is nothing to win.
How to play: Drag the dot, or focus it and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). Change the number of sides, tick Show hint to see why, or press Reset to start over.

Green and blue triangles alternate. Move P and watch the two totals.

Look for the math

Move the dot anywhere inside the polygon and the two totals stay level. That is not a coincidence or a rounding trick: it is a fact about every regular polygon with an even number of sides.

The claim, exactly

Let P be a point inside a regular 2n-gon. Drawing a line from P to each corner splits the polygon into 2n triangles, numbered around the shape. The page says the odd-numbered triangles and the even-numbered triangles have equal total area, and the logic test confirmed it for every option from 2n = 4 to 2n = 30 over 5,614 positions of P:

Area(even triangles) = Area(odd triangles) = Area(polygon) / 2

The original page has a typo, "split the letter", where it means the polygon; the claim here is the one its theorem states.

Equal sides turn areas into distances

Every triangle has one side of the polygon as its base, and that base has the same length s for all of them. Its height is the distance from P to that side line, so each area is (s / 2) × distance. Comparing the two totals is now just comparing two sums of distances. The test checked this identity triangle by triangle in every configuration, including feet that land beyond the ends of a side.

Two polygons hiding in the sides

Extend the even-numbered sides and they meet as one regular n-gon; extend the odd-numbered sides and they meet as another. Tick Show hint to see both. Each has the same apothem h as the original polygon, and the sum of distances from an inside point to the sides of a regular polygon is n × h — the generalization of Viviani's theorem. The two constants are therefore equal, and each total area is (s / 2) × n × h. The test checked that the two extended shapes really are congruent regular n-gons with apothem h for every 2n ≥ 6.

What if P leaves the polygon?

The page only claims the equality for a point inside. Drag P outside and the ordinary areas need no longer match: the triangles now overlap and the status line says so. If the distances are given signs — positive on the inside of a side line, negative on the outside — the two sums stay equal for any position of P, because the outward normals of the even sides add to zero and so do those of the odd sides. The test checked both facts. For a 4n-gon there is a simpler view, noted by Matt Henderson on the page: opposite sides are the same distance apart, so each pair of opposite triangles contributes equally.

Try N = 6 with the hint on: the two extended triangles make a six-pointed star around the hexagon, and the three solid and three dashed altitudes pair up across it.
